agri-tech-advisor.intro: Learn to advise farmers with modern tools — soil science, crop management, drones, sensors, and data. Agriculture employs more West Africans than any other sector. This career makes it productive.

skillDomains.name: Agronomy
skillDomains.description: The science of growing crops well.

skills.name: Soil Science
skills.description: Understand the ground beneath every crop.

modules.title: What soil actually is
modules.content:
Soil is not just dirt. It's a living system of:

  • Minerals — sand, silt, clay
  • Organic matter — decomposed plants and animals
  • Organisms — bacteria, fungi, worms, insects
  • Air and water — in the spaces between particles

Healthy soil has all four in balance. Degraded soil has too much of one and not enough of the others.

West African soils

Many are laterite — iron-rich, acidic, low in organic matter. Productive only with careful management of organic matter and pH.

modules.title: Reading the soil
modules.content:
Simple field tests

  • pH test — test strips or a meter. Most crops want 6.0-7.0.
  • Texture test — squeeze moist soil. Clay holds shape, sand crumbles, loam is in between.
  • Infiltration test — dig a small hole, pour water, time how long it takes to drain. Slow = compacted.
  • Earthworm count — dig a 30cm cube and count. Five or more = healthy biology.

What to do about it

Acidic soil: add lime or wood ash. Compacted soil: add organic matter and avoid heavy tillage. Low organic matter: compost, mulch, cover crops.

steps.q: A farmer's maize leaves are yellowing on lower leaves only. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Yellowing on older leaves = mobile nutrient deficiency, most often nitrogen.

steps.q: Water pools on the surface for hours after rain. What's the problem?
steps.f: Slow drainage = compaction. Break it up with deep-rooted cover crops or mechanical aeration.

steps.q: A soil test shows pH 4.5. What do you advise?
o: Add lime to raise pH toward 6.0-6.5
steps.f: At pH 4.5, most nutrients are locked up. Lime first, then fertilize.

modules.title: Choosing the right crop
modules.content:
Every farm decision starts with three questions:

  1. What grows well here? — matching crop to climate, soil, and water
  2. What does the market want? — a crop nobody buys is a loss
  3. What can the farmer manage? — labour, capital, and knowledge matter

Common West African crops

  • Maize, rice, sorghum, millet (staples)
  • Cassava, yam, sweet potato (roots)
  • Cowpea, groundnut, soybean (legumes — fix nitrogen)
  • Tomato, pepper, okra, onion (vegetables, high value)
  • Cocoa, oil palm, cashew (export)

modules.title: Pests and diseases
modules.content:
The big four for West African staples

  • Fall armyworm — attacks maize, devastating if untreated
  • Striga — parasitic weed that destroys cereals
  • Cassava mosaic virus — spreads by whitefly
  • Tomato leaf blight — kills tomato crops in days

Integrated pest management (IPM)

  1. Prevent — resistant varieties, crop rotation, clean seed
  2. Monitor — walk the field weekly, look for early signs
  3. Act early — hand-pick, spray botanical or chemical only if threshold is passed
  4. Rotate chemicals — prevents resistance

steps.q: Maize leaves have ragged holes and frass (droppings) in the whorl. What is it?
steps.f: Ragged holes plus frass in the leaf whorl is classic fall armyworm damage.

steps.q: Small purple-pink flowers growing among your maize, stunting it. What is it?
steps.f: Striga attaches to cereal roots and drains nutrients. Hand-pull before flowering.

steps.q: Tomato leaves have dark spots that spread rapidly and kill the plant in a week. What is it?
steps.f: Rapid dark spots = blight. Remove affected plants immediately and apply fungicide.

skillDomains.name: Data & Tools
skillDomains.description: Modern technology that multiplies a farmer's reach.

modules.title: What drones do for agriculture
modules.content:
Monitoring

Multispectral cameras on drones reveal crop stress days before the human eye can see it. Maps show exactly which parts of a field need attention.

Spraying

Spray drones cover a hectare in minutes with far less chemical than manual spraying — a huge saving on inputs and health risk.

Cost and licensing

A basic mapping drone costs 300,000-800,000 Le. Spray drones cost much more. In most West African countries you need to register the drone and hold a licence for commercial use.

You don't need to own a drone to be an advisor. Renting or partnering with a drone operator is normal.

modules.title: Advise on a drone service
modules.prompt: A cooperative of 30 farmers wants to know if drone spraying is worth it. Each farm is 1-2 hectares. Describe what you'd advise them and how you'd approach the decision.
modules.context: Technology adoption depends on economics, not novelty. Real advice weighs cost against benefit.
rubric: Calculates labour cost saved per hectare
Compares to manual or backpack sprayer cost
Considers whether one shared drone service for all 30 farms makes sense
Checks drone regulations in the country
Recommends based on numbers, not enthusiasm

skills.name: Record Keeping
skills.description: Data is a farm's memory. Without records, every season starts blind.

modules.title: What farmers should record
modules.content:
Every season

  • Planting date and variety
  • Inputs: seed, fertilizer, pesticide, amounts and costs
  • Labour hours and wages
  • Weather notes
  • Pest and disease events
  • Harvest date, quantity, and price

Why it matters

After three seasons of records a farmer knows:

  • Which variety performs best on their land
  • Whether fertilizer pays for itself
  • Which month yields highest price

Data turns experience into knowledge.

steps.q: A farmer says they can't read or write. How do they keep records?
o: Voice memos on a phone, or a family member helps
steps.f: Voice notes on any phone, a literate family member, or pictorial records all work. Records aren't only for the literate.

steps.q: You're advising a farmer who has 3 years of records. What's the most valuable thing they can do?
o: Compare yield and cost across seasons to find what works
steps.f: Comparing seasons reveals what works. This is the payoff of record keeping.

steps.q: When should a farmer record the labour cost of weeding?
o: At the end of the season
steps.f: Same-day recording. Memory fades and estimates drift.

skillDomains.name: Farmer Communication
skillDomains.description: Advice only matters if farmers act on it.

skills.name: Extension Methods
skills.description: How to teach adults who've farmed longer than you've studied.

modules.title: Adults learn by doing
modules.content:
Farmers do not want to be lectured. They want to see something work.

The farmer field school method

  1. Bring farmers together on one field
  2. Show two plots side by side — one with new method, one with old
  3. Let the group observe, measure, and discuss
  4. Agree on what to try next season

Evidence from their own field beats any recommendation from a book.

The rule

Never tell a farmer they're wrong. Show them the alternative and let them decide.

steps.q: A farmer says "my grandfather farmed this way, it works". What do you do?
o: Acknowledge their knowledge and propose a small trial on part of the field
steps.f: Respect tradition, test change. A small side-by-side trial does the arguing for you.

steps.q: You've recommended a new variety. The farmer is hesitant about cost. What's your approach?
o: Show the math: cost of seed vs expected yield
Give them the seed for free
steps.f: Numbers convince. Show yield per hectare, price per kg, and total return.

steps.q: A female farmer says men in the cooperative won't listen to her. What do you do?
o: Ensure her trial plots are visible and her results get equal attention
steps.f: Visible results from her plots change minds. Extension is not neutral — actively amplify women's successes.

skillDomains.name: Post-Harvest
skillDomains.description: Up to 40% of West African harvest is lost after picking. This is where advisors add value.

skills.name: Storage
skills.description: Keep the harvest safe from pests and moisture.

modules.title: Where harvest is lost
modules.content:
Losses happen from:

  • Insects — weevils, beetles, moths
  • Rodents — rats, mice
  • Moisture — mould, aflatoxin
  • Heat — spoilage
  • Theft — unprotected storage

Solutions

  • Hermetic storage bags (GrainPro, PICS) — sealed from oxygen, kills insects without chemicals
  • Metal silos — pest and rodent proof
  • Proper drying before storage — target moisture: 13% for maize
  • Raised, dry, ventilated storage rooms

Hermetic bags alone reduce losses from 30% to under 2%.

modules.title: Advise on storage
modules.prompt: A farmer harvested 5 tonnes of maize. They currently store in jute sacks in a wooden shed. They lose roughly 25% to weevils each year. What do you recommend?
modules.context: Post-harvest loss reduction is often more profitable than increasing yield.

skillDomains.name: Reporting
skillDomains.description: Turn farm data into reports that fund decisions.

skills.name: Report Writing
skills.description: Write reports NGOs, cooperatives, and governments actually read.

modules.title: Structure of a good report
modules.content:
Standard structure

  1. Executive summary — the main finding in 3 sentences
  2. Background — what was assessed and why
  3. Method — how data was collected
  4. Findings — with charts and numbers
  5. Recommendations — specific, actionable
  6. Appendix — raw data, photos

Most people only read the executive summary and the recommendations. Write them first, and write them well.

modules.title: Write a real field report
modules.prompt: Visit a real farm or use a simulated case. Produce a one-page report: findings and recommendations. It should be something the farmer or their cooperative can actually use.
steps: Include one chart showing the key numbers
Keep the executive summary under 100 words
